title: How to Improve Your Credit Score Before Applying for a Mortgage
description: Small credit moves in the months before you apply can make a real difference in your mortgage options. Here's what helps, what hurts, and what to avoid.
image_alt: A black credit card with a chip on a white background

faq.q: How far ahead should I work on my credit?
faq.a: Ideally three to six months before you apply. Some changes, like lower card balances, can show up within a billing cycle or two.

faq.q: Will shopping for a mortgage hurt my credit?
faq.a: Credit scoring models generally treat multiple mortgage inquiries within a short shopping window as one inquiry, so comparing lenders typically has a limited impact.

faq.q: Should I close old credit cards?
faq.a: Usually not before applying. Closing a card can raise your utilization and shorten your credit history, which can lower your score.

body_html:
Your credit score affects more than whether you're approved. It shapes pricing, mortgage insurance cost, and sometimes which programs are available. The good news: a few smart moves in the months before you apply can make a noticeable difference, and most of them are free.

Know where you're starting

Pull your credit reports from all three bureaus at AnnualCreditReport.com, the official free source. Look for accounts you don't recognize, late payments reported in error, and balances that are out of date. Disputing real errors is one of the fastest ways to improve a score.

Keep in mind that the score in your banking app may not match what a mortgage lender sees. Mortgage lending uses specific scoring models, so ask your loan officer for a review rather than relying on a free score alone.

The biggest lever: credit utilization

Utilization is the share of your available revolving credit you're using. High balances relative to limits can weigh down your score even if you pay in full every month, because many cards report the statement balance.

  • Pay balances down before the statement closing date, not just the due date
  • Spread balances across cards rather than maxing out one
  • Ask for a credit limit increase on an older card, if it won't trigger a hard inquiry

What helps and what hurts

HelpsHurts
On-time payments, every account, every monthAny new late payment, especially during the loan process
Lower card balancesMaxed-out cards
Keeping older accounts openClosing your oldest card
Fixing reporting errorsOpening new accounts right before applying
Setting up autopay on minimumsCollections left unresolved without a plan

Collections and old debts: be strategic

Paying an old collection doesn't always raise your score, and in some situations the timing matters. Some loan programs require certain collections to be paid; others don't. Talk with your loan officer before paying old accounts so you know whether it helps the approval, the score, both, or neither.

Don't make these moves during the process

  1. Don't open new credit cards or store accounts, even for a discount at checkout.
  2. Don't finance furniture, appliances, or a car before closing.
  3. Don't co-sign for anyone.
  4. Don't miss a payment because of moving chaos. Autopay is your friend.

Lenders often recheck credit right before closing. A new debt can change your debt-to-income ratio and delay or derail the loan.

Rapid rescoring

If you pay down a balance or correct an error mid-process, your lender may be able to request a rapid rescore, which updates your score faster than waiting for the next reporting cycle. It's not available for every situation, but it's worth asking about when a small change could improve your pricing.

A 90-day credit plan

If you're about three months from applying, here's a simple plan that works for most people:

  1. Week 1: Pull all three reports, list every account, and note balances, limits, and any errors.
  2. Weeks 2 to 4: File disputes for genuine errors and set up autopay on every account.
  3. Weeks 4 to 8: Pay revolving balances down, prioritizing cards closest to their limits. Pay before statement dates.
  4. Weeks 8 to 12: Avoid new credit entirely, then have your loan officer review your credit and discuss whether any targeted move could help further.

This won't fix everything, but it addresses the factors most likely to move in a short window.

Thin credit files

Some buyers don't have bad credit; they have very little of it. Young buyers, recent immigrants, and people who pay cash for everything often fall into this group. Options can include adding an authorized user account, opening a secured card well ahead of applying, or using programs that consider nontraditional credit like rent and utility payment history. Start early, because new accounts need time to age before they help.

The takeaway

Better credit is mostly about consistency: on-time payments, low balances, and no surprises. Start three to six months out if you can, and loop in your loan officer early so every move you make supports the loan you're aiming for.
